title: Rabbi Chalafta (Abba Chalafta)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-prepared translation; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: The father of the well-known tanna Rabbi Yosi, and a descendant of Yonadav ben Rechav, as stated in the [Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit 4:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.4.2.13).[^1]

He is mentioned once in the Mishnah, in [Taanit 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Taanit.2.5): “It happened in the days of Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradyon that someone went before the ark and completed the entire blessing, and they did not answer ‘Amen’ after him.”

He was already alive in the time of the Temple and saw Rabban Gamliel the Elder, as his son testifies in [Shabbat 115a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.115a.7). Rabbi Yosi said: “It happened that Abba Chalafta”—Rashi explains that Rabbi Yosi’s father was named Chalafta—“went to Rabban Gamliel Beribbi in Tiberias and found him sitting at the table of Rabbi Yohanan ben Nizuf. He said to him: ‘I remember your grandfather, Rabban Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount,’” and so forth. The account also appears near the beginning of [Tosefta Shabbat, chapter 14](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Shabbat.14.2), and in [Soferim 5:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Tractate_Soferim.5.15).[^2]

Now, since he had lived to see Rabban Gamliel the Elder, he must have been over thirty at the time of the destruction. Nevertheless, the Gemara in [Bava Kamma 70a–70b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.70a.16-70b.3) is uncertain about the following account: Rabbi Yosi said, “When Abba Chalafta went to Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri to study Torah”—or, according to another version, Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri went to Abba Chalafta—“he said to him: ‘Suppose he enjoyed its produce …’”; the account continues, “But Rabbi Akiva disagrees about this.”[^3]

In [Tosefta Maaser Sheni 1:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Maaser_Sheni.1.13) and [Tosefta Bava Batra 2:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Bava_Batra.2.4), Rabbi Yosi says: “Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri came to [Abba] Chalafta … He said to him: ‘I too say so, but Akiva says …’” Likewise, in [Tosefta Oholot, chapter 5](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Oholot.5.7), Rabbi Yosi says: “Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri came to Abba Chalafta … ‘But Akiva declares it pure.’” From this we see that he was Rabbi Akiva’s colleague, since he called him simply “Akiva.” This is because his period of activity is reckoned with the generation of Rabbi Akiva and his associates, like that entire generation, whose members had also lived before the destruction.[^4]

He was the head in Sepphoris, as is stated in [Rosh Hashanah 27a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.27a.13) and [Taanit 16b](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.16b.10): “This was Rabbi Chalafta’s practice in Sepphoris.” His colleague Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradyon was then the head in Sikhni, as stated there.[^5]

We have found no students attributed to him. Only his son Rabbi Yosi regularly mentions him as “Abba Chalafta,” as cited above. We also find in [Sotah 34a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.34a.8): “R. Y. said: Abba Chalafta, Rabbi Eliezer ben Matya, and Hananiah ben Hakhinai stood on those stones,” and so forth. (Possibly the meaning is that these three sages stood on the stones, but at different times, since Hananiah ben Hakhinai lived later than Rabbi Chalafta.)[^6]

In [Sanhedrin 80a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.80a.1-2), Rabbi Yosi says, “Even if Abba Chalafta is among them.” And in [Meilah 17b](https://www.sefaria.org/Meilah.17b.2), Rabbi Yosi says: “If Abba Chalafta were alive, could you say to him, ‘Give your son over to be killed’?”[^7]

It appears that he lived a long life. At the beginning of [Tosefta Kelim, Bava Batra, chapter 2](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Kelim_Batra.2.1), Rabbi Yosi says: “It happened that four elders were sitting privately with Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah in Sepphoris: Rabbi Hutzpit the interpreter, Rabbi Yeshavav, and Rabbi [read: Abba] Chalafta.” This undoubtedly took place when the revolt of Betar began, or afterward.[^8]
His son Rabbi Yosi succeeded to his father’s position in Sepphoris, as explained in [his entry](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-867aecd23abaf7b4).

He also had another son, who died without children. Rabbi Yosi, the deceased man’s brother, married his widow in levirate marriage, as stated at the beginning of [the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.1.1.6). Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta, however, was not his son, as explained in [that entry](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-1e5e408c4fbf54df).[^9]

notes.text: The linked Yerushalmi directly identifies **Rabbi Yosi son of Chalafta** as a descendant of Yonadav ben Rechav. Hyman accordingly applies this ancestry to Chalafta. This translation retains Hyman’s genealogical conclusion as his conclusion; the source does not name Chalafta’s father. “Abba Chalafta” here refers to Rabbi Yosi’s father, explicitly identified in [Rashi on Shabbat 115a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Shabbat.115a).

Hyman prints “Rabbi Yohanan **ben Nizuf**”; the linked Bavli reads **Yohanan ha-Nazuf**, “Yohanan the censured.” The Tosefta has its own variant, “Yohanan [ben Nozef].” The translation preserves Hyman’s wording rather than silently substituting the Bavli’s form. In Hyman’s account, Chalafta is the speaker who recalls the elder Gamliel. “Beribbi” is retained as a designation of distinction; it has not been converted into a patronymic. Modern subsection numbers are supplied for convenience; Hyman cites the beginning of Tosefta Shabbat’s chapter 14.

The uncertainty concerns **who visited whom**, not whether Chalafta existed or was Rabbi Yosi’s father. The abbreviated quotation concerns enjoying a field’s produce as evidence for a claim of possession. The story begins at the end of Bava Kamma 70a and continues on 70b; Hyman’s citation to 70a is correct. [Bava Batra 56b:3–4](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.56b.3-4) is a parallel, not a correction to his reference. The age “over thirty” is Hyman’s historical inference; the quoted narrative itself gives no age or birth date.

The brackets around “[Abba]” reproduce Hyman’s editorial intervention. The retrieved Tosefta Bava Batra and Oholot texts have **Rabbi Chalafta**, while Maaser Sheni has **Chalafta** without a title. These versions have not been harmonized in the Hebrew transcription. Hyman groups several related reports into a compressed quotation; they concern different legal subjects. His inference that the unadorned name “Akiva” indicates a colleague is retained as an inference, not independently demonstrated here.

Hyman uses **הריש**, “the head,” for each sage. The linked passages explicitly describe their instituting or following a communal practice; they do not independently state a formal appointment to an office. “Head” therefore preserves Hyman’s characterization without specifying an otherwise unattested institutional title.

Hyman abbreviates the reporting sage’s name as **אר״י**, left here as “R. Y.” The fetched Sotah text reads **Rabbi Yehuda**. It should not be expanded to “Rabbi Yosi” solely because the surrounding paragraphs quote Yosi. “Those stones” are the stones associated with the Israelites’ crossing of the Jordan. The suggestion that the three men visited them at different times is Hyman’s own parenthetical explanation.

“Even if Abba Chalafta is among them” belongs to a **hypothetical legal discussion**; it is not an allegation that Chalafta committed an offense. The statement in Meilah is likewise counterfactual and concerns the danger of a mission under Roman persecution. The translation does not turn either statement into a biographical event.

The scan explicitly identifies the Tosefta subdivision as **Kelim, Bava Batra**; the existing Wikisource transcription omits “Bava Batra.” The modern Sefaria title is *Tosefta Kelim Batra*. The unpointed word **חרש** is read adverbially here as “privately”; it does not describe Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah as a craftsman. Hyman quotes only part of the list; the cited Tosefta also names **Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri** as the fourth elder. Hyman’s bracketed replacement of “Rabbi” with “Abba,” and his confident dating to the revolt centered on Betar, remain his editorial and historical judgments. They have not been promoted to independently verified corrections or dates.

The Yerushalmi explicitly says that Rabbi Yosi ben Chalafta married his brother’s widow. The brother is unnamed there. Hyman’s rejection of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta as a son, and his account of Yosi’s succession in Sepphoris, refer the reader to other biographies; neither is independently established by this one passage. The links preserve those cross-references without merging the people concerned.
